subject: turtle
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module to build a sea turtle model using the SDK, aiming for a realistic scale of about 1 meter carapace length, oriented facing +Z with flippers resting at ground level.

I'm sketching the joint hierarchy: a root body joint, a neck chain leading to a head joint with hinged jaw bones, and flipper chains built from shoulder-elbow-wrist joints, considering extrude outlines to shape the paddle-like flipper blades.

Working out the flipper orientations — defining x/y direction vectors so the front flippers extend sideways as flat paddles, while the smaller hind flippers angle back and outward with their own perpendicular axes.

For the front flipper outline, I'm sketching paddle-shaped points that narrow at the root and widen toward a rounded tip, with thin extrusion and a small bevel for smoothness.

Now I'm thinking about how to build the carapace itself — considering a lathe or loft approach to create the flattened, elongated dome shape typical of a sea turtle's shell.

Defining loft stations...

I need the shell bottom and flipper tips to satisfy the floor-contact rule — lowest point must rest at roughly y=0. I'll aim for the shell bottom around y=0.03 and angle the flipper paddles so their tips graze the ground near y=0, accepting this as an approximation since I can't verify exact numeric placement.

I'm setting the shell's cross-section heights so the bottom sinks slightly below ground level while tapering smoothly, keeping overall carapace proportions around 0.85m long and 0.66m wide to match a sea turtle's build. For the shell texture I'm planning to use a scute pattern with a scales paint, mixing olive-green base tones with cream edges to mimic hexagonal carapace plates.

For shading, I'm considering a conditional paint function that switches between the scute pattern on top and a lighter cream tone underneath based on surface normal direction, giving a stylized plastron edge without needing a separate geometric piece. Now I'm moving on to shaping the head.

For the head, I'm thinking of a simple sphere joint attached at the neck end, with small dark eyes and a beak formed from upper and lower jaw plates extruded in the side profile (z-y plane) with thickness running sideways along X. I'm placing the head roughly at z=0.62, y=0.2, larger than the neck, with the neck rising from the shell's front edge up to that point.

Now I'm setting up the root joint for the body, then building a neck chain parented to it with a few intermediate joints running from the shell front to the head, and sweeping a tapered tube along that chain for the neck geometry.

Still placing jaw and eye joints...

I'll give the loft a "head" bone reference so it attaches properly despite overlapping with the neck chain's tip. For the front flippers, I'm setting up a three-joint chain (shoulder, elbow, wrist) tagged as an "arm" role, then sweeping it with tapering radius and skin-tone color to form the paddle shape.

Placing the shoulder joint inside the shell near the lower side so the flipper looks like it emerges naturally, then working out elbow and wrist positions so the paddle sits just above ground level without clipping through the shell. Now I'm working out the paddle's extrusion orientation at the wrist joint, adjusting its direction and up vectors so the paddle plane sits correctly relative to the body.

I'm figuring out the orthogonal basis vectors for the paddle's extrusion frame, then defining the flipper's outline points and surface mottling to give it a textured skin look, and sketching the hind flipper chain similarly with a smaller paddle. I'm setting up side-mirroring logic so both left and right limbs share the same geometry with flipped x-coordinates, then laying out the tail chain and adjusting its height so it clears the ground.

Now I'm working through the shell's cross-section stations (width, height, z-position) to loft a smooth, slightly flattened dome shape, making sure the bottom sits right at ground level without excessive floating, and choosing enough sides so the loft doesn't look too faceted. I'm deciding to skip a visible plastron since it sits against the ground, but considering a cream-colored rim and head coloring with a subtle olive tone, plus adding spherical eyes with slightly protruding pupils for a bead-like look.

I'm building the beak as an extrusion from the head joint, working out outline coordinates for a hooked upper beak shape and a separate lower jaw extrusion so the mouth can later be posed open, making sure the orientation vectors give the correct thickness direction and width. I'm also defining the root body joint position, deciding against a separate spine chain for simplicity, and working out the tail and neck joint chains, counting points and spans to make sure joint names and tip positions align correctly.

I'm checking the neck chain's catmull interpolation and joint tip orientation, then setting up the arm and leg chains with explicit joint names and parent bindings, verifying that shoulder, elbow, and wrist positions sit appropriately relative to the shell's cross-section so the flippers visibly emerge from the sides rather than staying buried inside. I'm doing similar placement checks for the hind legs, confirming the knee and ankle fall outside the shell's silhouette, and adjusting flipper proportions for a realistic turtle-like span of around two meters.

For the head, I'm defining loft stations with position, width, and height to build a rounded skull shape with a tapered snout, then checking eye placement against the head's cross-sectional ellipse so the eye spheres sit just proud of the surface rather than sunken in. I'm working out the neck and limb sweep radii for appropriately thick proportions, and writing paint functions -- one using a scute-like scale pattern with darker edge tones for the shell, and a lighter cream underside, plus a mottled green tone for the flippers.

I'm weighing whether to add small claw spikes to the flipper tips but deciding to skip them to avoid misplacement risk, and instead double-checking that the lowest points of the model -- flipper paddles, head, shell bottom -- sit close enough to the ground plane within the allowed tolerance, adjusting wrist and ankle heights accordingly. I'm also sanity-checking overall model proportions (shell length, height, flipper span) against real sea turtle anatomy.

Now I'm writing the actual builder code: setting up metadata and a default export function that constructs the model and returns the root, importing the necessary modules, then writing a loop over left/right sides that builds mirrored arm chains using catmull-interpolated joint positions, sweeps them into tapered limb geometry with skin-colored material, and retrieves the wrist joint to use as the attachment frame for the paddle extrusion with the correct orientation vectors.

Writing paddle outline vertices...

I'm working out a mirrored coordinate system so the paddle's local x/y directions stay orthogonal for both left and right sides, then reasoning through winding order to make sure normals don't flip when mirrored, confirming the rotation basis stays right-handed so there's no accidental reflection artifact.

Writing hind leg chain and paddle outline...

I'm defining the shell's loft stations with position, width, and height values tapering from the rear to the front, computing vertical offsets so each ellipse section sits correctly relative to its own height, and setting the shell material to the scute paint pattern with a rounded polygon cross-section. I'm doing the same for the head loft, retrieving the neck chain's tip joint to use as the head's attachment bone, then sweeping the neck itself with a tapering radius and skin color.

I'm building the jaw joint and beak geometry next, placing the upper and lower beak extrusions with outline points sized to form a slightly open beak shape, picking a muted olive-brown color for the beak material, and checking that the jaw and upper beak don't gap or clip awkwardly at the mouth line.

Writing beak outline coordinates...

I'm adding small eye and pupil spheres positioned on the head's surface using explicit bone binding, then building a tail chain that starts inside the shell and tapers out past the rear opening, sweeping it with a thin skin-colored tube. I'm finalizing material choices, making sure type signatures for chain names, outline points, and radius arrays line up with the SDK's expected input shapes, and preparing to write out the complete file in one pass.
